summary:
Jay cannot ship to testers today. Verified on his machine: the only codesigning identity present is `Apple Development: jayhpateluk@icloud.com (WALY2J97BF)` — there is no Developer ID Application certificate, and `xcrun notarytool history` returns "Must provide credentials", so no notary credentials are configured either. An Apple Development-signed app is not a distribution artifact; on macOS 15+ Apple removed the right-click→Open Gatekeeper bypass, so testers would hit an admin-authenticated "Open Anyway" flow in System Settings, and on macOS 26 (Jay's own OS) that is the only path. Everything else follows from fixing that.

Three concrete defects in the existing pipeline, all verified by reading `/Users/jaypatel/Vault/baps.solutions/w1.baps.solutions/packaging/build.sh` and `packaging/w1.entitlements`: (1) the codesign invocation has no `--timestamp`, and a secure timestamp is mandatory for notarization — this alone will fail every submission; (2) it uses `codesign --deep`, deprecated since macOS 13 and which sprays the same entitlements and the same `--identifier health.baps.w1` across all 336 nested Mach-O files found in the venv; (3) the entitlements set both `allow-jit` and `allow-unsigned-executable-memory`, which Apple DTS explicitly says not to do ("Only set one of these entitlements, because each is a superset of its predecessor").

On the Python/MLX question specifically: w1 genuinely needs `allow-unsigned-executable-memory`, not `allow-jit`. sounddevice drives PortAudio callbacks through CFFI `ffi.callback()`, which allocates libffi write+execute closures that `allow-jit` (MAP_JIT + pthread_jit_write_protect) does not cover — the documented failure is `MemoryError: Cannot allocate write+execute memory for ffi.callback()`. PyObjC's own docs confirm it generates executable stubs needing a hardened-runtime exception. Drop `allow-jit`, keep `allow-unsigned-executable-memory`. MLX does not add a JIT requirement: `mlx/lib/mlx.metallib` is a 157 MB *precompiled* Metal library (verified locally), loaded as data, not JIT-compiled in-process.

Model weights: verified 1.5 GB in `~/.cache/huggingface/hub/models--mlx-community--whisper-large-v3-turbo`, 1.61 GB on Hugging Face. Keep downloading on first run. Bundling pushes each release over ~2 GB, and large binaries have been reported taking 3.5–4.5 hours to notarize against a 75-submissions-per-day cap — that would destroy Jay's iteration loop for zero user benefit, since the weights never change between releases.

Channels: signed+notarized DMG plus Sparkle from day one. TestFlight is genuinely unavailable — it requires a Mac App Store build uploaded to App Store Connect, which requires the sandbox, which is incompatible with Accessibility-based paste injection and Input Monitoring. Official homebrew-cask is also out (needs 75 stars/30 forks/30 watchers, or 225/90/90 self-submitted), though Jay's own tap has no such gate and is a fine secondary channel for technical testers.

The sharpest non-technical risk is the privacy promise. "100% on-device, nothing leaves the Mac" is already not literally true — first run fetches 1.5 GB from Hugging Face — and three planned features break it structurally. A bot that joins Teams/Meet/Zoom as a participant is the worst offender: the standard implementation is a server-side headless client, which means meeting audio leaves the user's Mac entirely. Jay should move from one global claim to per-feature data-flow statements plus a hard "strict local" toggle before he ships to clinicians who may dictate patient material.

findings.topic: No Developer ID certificate exists — this is the hard blocker
findings.detail: `security find-identity -v -p codesigning` on Jay's machine returns exactly one identity: `Apple Development: jayhpateluk@icloud.com (WALY2J97BF)`, '1 valid identities found'. An Apple Development certificate is a *development* identity — it is not accepted by the notary service and does not produce a Gatekeeper-clean app on someone else's Mac. Notarization requires a Developer ID Application certificate. Apple further states you must be the Account Holder of the team to generate one, which for an individual enrollment Jay would be by default. Developer ID Application certs are valid 5 years. Jay should also create a Developer ID Installer cert at the same time if he ever wants to ship a .pkg. Critically, the private key must be backed up as a .p12 offline — Apple limits how many Developer ID certs an account can hold, and losing the key is a support-ticket-grade problem.
findings.evidence: Local: `security find-identity -v -p codesigning` → only 'Apple Development: jayhpateluk@icloud.com (WALY2J97BF)'. https://developer.apple.com/developer-id/ ('you must be the Account Holder of your development team in the Apple Developer Program in order to generate this certificate'). https://developer.apple.com/help/account/certificates/create-developer-id-certificates/

findings.topic: Apple Developer Program membership status could NOT be verified
findings.detail: I cannot determine from the shell whether team WALY2J97BF is a paid Apple Developer Program team or a free Xcode 'personal team'. Both issue certificates named identically (`Apple Development: <email> (TEAMID)`), so the local keychain gives no signal. This matters because a free personal team cannot create a Developer ID certificate at all. Jay must check appleid/developer.apple.com directly. If he needs to enrol: $99/yr, and individual enrollment does NOT require a D-U-N-S number (only organization enrollment does). Individual enrollment is faster; the tradeoff is that his personal legal name, not 'BAPS Solutions', appears as the signer in Gatekeeper dialogs and in `codesign -dv` output. If he wants the company name in front of testers he needs org enrollment plus a D-U-N-S, which adds days-to-weeks.
findings.evidence: Unverifiable locally — no shell command exposes program membership tier. https://developer.apple.com/programs/enroll/ and https://developer.apple.com/help/account/membership/D-U-N-S/ (D-U-N-S required for organizations, not individuals/sole proprietors).

findings.topic: notarytool has no stored credentials — use an App Store Connect API key, not an app-specific password
findings.detail: `xcrun notarytool history` returns 'Error: Must provide credentials.' There is no keychain profile and no .p8 under ~/.appstoreconnect/private_keys/. Recommended setup: create an App Store Connect API key (Users and Access → Integrations), download the .p8 once (it is not re-downloadable), note the Key ID and Issuer ID, then `xcrun notarytool store-credentials "w1-notary" --key /path/AuthKey_KEYID.p8 --key-id KEYID --issuer ISSUER-UUID --validate`. Thereafter submit with `-p w1-notary`. Do NOT mix `--apple-id`/`--team-id` with `--key` — notarytool errors out. API key is preferable to an app-specific password because it is scoped, revocable without touching Jay's Apple ID, survives Apple ID password changes, and is the only sane option if notarization ever moves to CI. notarytool accepts only three upload formats: UDIF disk images, signed flat installer packages, and zip archives — a bare .app cannot be submitted.
findings.evidence: Local: `xcrun notarytool history` → 'Error: Must provide credentials.' https://keith.github.io/xcode-man-pages/notarytool.1.html (store-credentials, auth options, 'UDIF disk images, signed "flat" installer packages, and zip files'). https://github.com/electron/notarize

findings.topic: build.sh is missing --timestamp — every notarization submission will fail
findings.detail: packaging/build.sh line: `codesign --force --deep --options runtime --entitlements ... --identifier health.baps.w1 --sign "$SIGN_ID"`. There is no `--timestamp` flag. A secure timestamp from Apple's timestamp server is a hard notarization requirement — without it the notary service rejects the submission with 'The signature does not include a secure timestamp.' This is a one-word fix but it is currently a guaranteed failure. `--options runtime` (hardened runtime) is correctly present.

findings.topic: codesign --deep is deprecated and wrong for a 336-binary Python bundle
findings.detail: `--deep` has been deprecated for signing since macOS 13. It recursively signs nested code but applies *all* signing options to *all* nested content — meaning Jay's `--entitlements w1.entitlements` and `--identifier health.baps.w1` get stamped onto every nested Mach-O, including libportaudio.dylib, libmlx.dylib, and every .so. Granting allow-unsigned-executable-memory to 336 separate binaries is far broader than intended, and giving them all the same identifier is incorrect. I counted 336 .so/.dylib/.metallib files under the site-packages tree that ends up in the bundle. Correct approach: sign inside-out — iterate all nested Mach-O files first with `codesign --force --timestamp --options runtime --sign "$ID"` (no entitlements, no identifier), then sign the outer .app last with the entitlements and identifier. Note macOS 10.9+ records nested code by its own signature in the outer resource envelope, so nested items must already be validly signed before the outer signing runs or it fails.
findings.evidence: Local: build.sh uses `--force --deep`; `find .venv_old_w4k/lib/python3.12/site-packages -name '*.so' -o -name '*.dylib' -o -name '*.metallib' | wc -l` → 336. https://keith.github.io/xcode-man-pages/codesign.1.html ('--deep ... is deprecated'). https://github.com/beeware/briefcase/issues/1221. https://developer.apple.com/library/archive/technotes/tn2206/_index.html

findings.topic: Entitlements: drop allow-jit, keep allow-unsigned-executable-memory — Apple says set only one
findings.detail: packaging/w1.entitlements currently sets allow-jit AND allow-unsigned-executable-memory AND disable-library-validation. Apple DTS (Quinn 'The Eskimo!'): 'This sequence is a trade off between increasing programmer convenience and decreasing security. com.apple.security.cs.allow-jit is the most secure... Only set one of these entitlements, because each is a superset of its predecessor.' For w1 the *required* one is allow-unsigned-executable-memory, not allow-jit: sounddevice's PortAudio callbacks go through CFFI `ffi.callback()`, which allocates libffi closures in write+execute memory. allow-jit only permits the MAP_JIT + `pthread_jit_write_with_callback_np` pattern, which libffi does not use — the documented symptom is `MemoryError: Cannot allocate write+execute memory for ffi.callback()`. PyObjC's own docs confirm it 'uses a limited form of dynamic code generation to create executable stubs... This requires an exception from the Hardened Runtime configuration.' Recommendation: keep only `com.apple.security.cs.allow-unsigned-executable-memory`; remove `allow-jit`. Separately, test whether `disable-library-validation` can be dropped — once every nested .so/.dylib is re-signed with Jay's own Developer ID (Team ID WALY2J97BF), library validation should be satisfied, and dropping it meaningfully narrows the attack surface. Also confirm `com.apple.security.get-task-allow` is absent from release builds; it blocks notarization.
findings.evidence: Local: packaging/w1.entitlements sets all three. https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/776290 (Quinn: 'Only set one of these entitlements, because each is a superset of its predecessor'). https://pyobjc.readthedocs.io/en/latest/notes/codesigning.html. https://github.com/spatialaudio/python-sounddevice/issues/270 (ffi.callback() in codesigned notarized app). https://bugs.python.org/issue42688

findings.topic: MLX does not need a JIT entitlement — its Metal library is precompiled
findings.detail: A reasonable worry is that MLX JIT-compiles Metal kernels and therefore needs allow-jit. It does not, in the default pip build. Verified locally: `.venv_old_w4k/lib/python3.12/site-packages/mlx/lib/` contains `mlx.metallib` at 157,748,008 bytes (157 MB), `libmlx.dylib` at 21 MB, and `libjaccl.dylib` at 930 KB. mlx.metallib is a *precompiled* GPU kernel library loaded as data — the MLX_METAL_JIT build flag that enables runtime kernel compilation is an opt-in that trades size for cold-start latency and is not what the pip wheel ships. Two consequences: (a) the JIT entitlement question is settled by libffi/PyObjC, not MLX; (b) MLX alone contributes 178 MB to the bundle before any Python, any weights, or any UI shell — worth knowing when Jay sizes the download.
findings.evidence: Local: `ls -la .venv_old_w4k/lib/python3.12/site-packages/mlx/lib/` → mlx.metallib 157748008 bytes, libmlx.dylib 21653808 bytes; `du -sh .../mlx` → 178M. https://ml-explore.github.io/mlx/build/html/install.html (MLX_METAL_JIT is an opt-in build flag that shrinks the metallib by runtime-compiling kernels)

findings.topic: Correct end-to-end notarization sequence for w1
findings.detail: 1) Build with py2app from a framework Python (already documented in docs/PACKAGING.md). 2) Strip xattrs: `ditto --norsrc --noextattr --noacl` — build.sh already does this and it matters, since iCloud FinderInfo xattrs make codesign reject the bundle as 'detritus'. 3) Sign every nested Mach-O inside-out: `codesign --force --timestamp --options runtime --sign "Developer ID Application: ... (WALY2J97BF)"` per file, no entitlements. 4) Sign the outer .app last, with `--entitlements packaging/w1.entitlements --identifier health.baps.w1 --timestamp --options runtime`. 5) `codesign --verify --strict --deep --verbose=2 dist/W1.app` and `spctl -a -vvv -t exec dist/W1.app`. 6) Zip for submission: `ditto -c -k --keepParent dist/W1.app W1.zip` (plain `zip` breaks symlinks/signatures). 7) `xcrun notarytool submit W1.zip -p w1-notary --wait`. On failure, `xcrun notarytool log <submission-id> -p w1-notary` gives per-file JSON reasons — this is the tool that actually tells you which of the 336 binaries was missed. 8) `xcrun stapler staple dist/W1.app`. 9) Build the DMG *from the stapled app*. 10) Notarize and staple the DMG too. Staple both: the ticket stapled to a DMG does not travel with the .app extracted from it, so stapling only the DMG leaves the installed app dependent on an online Gatekeeper check. 11) Verify offline: disconnect network, `spctl -a -vvv -t install W1.dmg`.
findings.evidence: https://keith.github.io/xcode-man-pages/notarytool.1.html. https://deciphertools.com/blog/notarizing-dmg/ (staple both app and dmg; ticket does not travel with extracted app). https://christiantietze.de/posts/2022/07/mac-app-notarization-workflow-in-2022/. Local: build.sh already implements the ditto xattr workaround.

findings.topic: Switching from Apple Development to Developer ID will reset all TCC grants — do it BEFORE any tester install
findings.detail: macOS TCC keys permission grants to the app's designated requirement, which encodes the signing identity and Team ID. Moving from `Apple Development: jayhpateluk@icloud.com` to `Developer ID Application: ... (WALY2J97BF)` changes that requirement, so existing Accessibility and Input Monitoring grants will not carry over. Worse, the stale entries often remain visible and *toggled on* in System Settings while being non-functional, so the user sees a granted permission that does nothing — the fix is to select the entry, press '−' to remove it, then re-add. This is exactly the failure mode Jay's build.sh comments already describe for ad-hoc signatures. Practical rule: get the Developer ID certificate first and never ship an Apple Development-signed build to a tester, because migrating them later means walking every tester through a manual TCC repair. Jay will need to do this once on his own machine.
findings.evidence: https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/785384 (Handling Permissions After Transferring macOS App to a New Developer ID). https://hacktricks.wiki/en/macos-hardening/macos-security-and-privilege-escalation/macos-security-protections/macos-tcc/index.html. Local: build.sh comments already document the ad-hoc/stable-identity problem.

findings.topic: macOS 15+ removed the right-click→Open bypass, which raises the cost of NOT notarizing
findings.detail: Through macOS 14, a tester could Control-click an unsigned or dev-signed app and choose Open to bypass Gatekeeper. macOS Sequoia removed that. The replacement flow is: attempt to open, get blocked, go to System Settings → Privacy & Security, scroll to find the app, click 'Open Anyway', then authenticate as an administrator. Jay is on macOS 26.0.1, so this is the present reality for anyone he ships to. For a dictation tool that *also* immediately demands Microphone, Accessibility, and Input Monitoring, stacking an admin-authenticated Gatekeeper override on top of three TCC grants is a brutal first-run experience and will cost him testers. Notarization removes exactly one of those four friction points — the one that makes the app look untrustworthy.

findings.topic: Entitlements and Info.plist keys the planned features actually require
findings.detail: Microphone — `com.apple.security.device.audio-input` entitlement (already present) plus `NSMicrophoneUsageDescription` (already present). Prompts automatically on first capture. Accessibility (paste injection, focus detection) — NO entitlement and NO Info.plist key exist; it is a manual System Settings toggle. Call `AXIsProcessTrustedWithOptions` with kAXTrustedCheckOptionPrompt to surface the 'Open System Settings' nudge. Input Monitoring (global Right-Option hotkey) — again no entitlement; use `IOHIDRequestAccess(kIOHIDRequestTypeListenEvent)` to trigger the prompt rather than silently receiving no events. Note pynput's listener needs this and fails silently without it. ScreenCaptureKit system audio — requires the 'Screen & System Audio Recording' TCC grant even for audio-only capture; the usual hack is a 2x2-pixel video stream with capturesAudio=true, and the app must be restarted after the grant before capture works. Core Audio process taps (macOS 14.4+) — the better option for meeting capture: narrower TCC scope, its own category separate from both microphone and screen recording, and it requires `NSAudioCaptureUsageDescription` in Info.plist (exact key confirmed against Apple's docs; note it is not in Xcode's dropdown and must be typed manually). There is no public API to query or request that permission — it is triggered by first use. Both capture paths require a stable signing identity because TCC keys the record off it, which is another argument for Developer ID before testers.

findings.topic: TestFlight is genuinely unavailable for w1 — not a judgement call, a structural block
findings.detail: TestFlight for macOS exists, but it distributes Mac App Store builds only: the app must be uploaded to App Store Connect signed for App Store distribution, not with Developer ID, and it must pass Beta App Review before external testers can install. Mac App Store builds require the App Sandbox. w1's core mechanics — Accessibility-API paste injection into arbitrary third-party apps, Input Monitoring for a global hotkey, and an always-on-top floating widget over other apps — are not achievable under the sandbox with a standard entitlement set. There is no path where a Developer ID-signed build reaches TestFlight. Rule it out and stop spending thought on it.
findings.evidence: https://developer.apple.com/testflight/ and https://developer.apple.com/developer-id/ (Developer ID is for direct distribution outside the store; TestFlight builds go through App Store Connect and Beta App Review). https://developer.apple.com/programs/

findings.topic: Distribution channels compared honestly for a small tester group
findings.detail: Signed+notarized DMG on an HTTPS URL — the right answer for early testers. Zero infrastructure, no Gatekeeper warning, works for non-technical users, and Jay controls who gets the link. Downside: updates are manual until Sparkle lands, and he has no idea who is on which version. Sparkle appcast — add this from day one, not later; retrofitting an updater after testers are on old builds is how you end up supporting five versions. Official homebrew-cask — effectively closed: general submissions need 30 forks / 30 watchers / 75 stars, and self-submitted casks need 90 / 90 / 225. w1 will not clear that bar as a private beta, and the cask would also have to point at a developer-published download anyway. Jay's own tap (`brew tap bkt-baps-solutions/tap` → `brew install --cask w1`) has no notability gate, is trivial to stand up from a GitHub repo, and is genuinely nice for technical testers — but it is a supplement to the DMG, not a replacement, because non-technical testers will not use it. TestFlight — unavailable (see separate finding). Recommendation: notarized DMG behind a link, plus Sparkle, plus an optional private tap for the developer-ish testers.
findings.evidence: https://docs.brew.sh/Acceptable-Casks and https://github.com/Homebrew/brew/blob/master/docs/Acceptable-Casks.md (notability thresholds; download must be developer-published). https://developer.apple.com/developer-id/

findings.topic: Auto-update: Sparkle, not the Tauri updater
findings.detail: Sparkle 2 is the correct choice and it works with a py2app/PyObjC bundle — the integration is pyobjc-core loading Sparkle.framework and driving SPUStandardUpdaterController (SUUpdater is deprecated in Sparkle 2; use the modern class). Two independent signatures are involved, and conflating them is the classic mistake: (a) Apple Developer ID codesigning of the app *and* of Sparkle's nested XPC services (Downloader.xpc, InstallerLauncher.xpc, InstallerConnection.xpc, InstallerStatus.xpc) plus Autoupdate.app — these add several more nested binaries to the inside-out signing loop; (b) Sparkle's own EdDSA signature over each update archive, generated by `bin/generate_keys` (private key stored in the login Keychain) with the public key embedded as `SUPublicEDKey` in Info.plist, and archives signed via `bin/sign_update` or automatically by `bin/generate_appcast`. Set `SUFeedURL` to an HTTPS appcast; HTTPS is required per App Transport Security. Sparkle additionally verifies the downloaded bundle's code signature matches the running app, so Developer ID consistency is load-bearing. The Tauri updater is only relevant if Jay adopts a Tauri shell for the new Tailwind/shadcn UI; it uses a separate minisign keypair (`tauri signer generate`, `TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY`, pubkey in tauri.conf.json, `.sig` files alongside a `.app.tar.gz`), and crucially it does NOT replace Developer ID signing or notarization — he would need minisign *and* Developer ID *and* notarization. Tauri also has known friction signing sidecar binaries (ExternalBin), which is exactly what a bundled Python engine would be. Verdict: Sparkle, regardless of shell choice, unless the shell is Tauri and he specifically wants one toolchain.
findings.evidence: https://sparkle-project.org/documentation/ (generate_keys, SUPublicEDKey, SUFeedURL, generate_appcast, HTTPS/ATS requirement). https://sparkle-project.org/documentation/upgrading/ (SUUpdater deprecated, use SPUStandardUpdaterController). https://deepwiki.com/sparkle-project/Sparkle/1-overview (XPC services). https://fman.io/blog/codesigning-and-automatic-updates-for-pyqt-apps/ (Sparkle from a Python app via pyobjc-core). https://v2.tauri.app/plugin/updater/ and https://v2.tauri.app/distribute/sign/macos/. https://github.com/tauri-apps/tauri/issues/11992

findings.topic: Model weights: 1.5 GB — keep downloading on first run, but fix the first-run experience
findings.detail: Verified real size: `du -sh ~/.cache/huggingface/hub/models--mlx-community--whisper-large-v3-turbo` → 1.5 GB locally; the HF repo lists weights.safetensors at 1.61 GB. Bundling it would take the app from roughly 400-500 MB (MLX alone is 178 MB, plus CPython, PyObjC, numpy) to over 2 GB. Consequences of bundling: every notarization submission uploads 2 GB+; large binaries have been reported taking 3.5-4.5 hours end-to-end versus minutes for normal ones; Apple documents a 75-notarizations-per-day limit, and long submissions make that ceiling real during a rapid beta; and Sparkle would push 2 GB to every tester on every release for weights that never changed. Downloading on first run (current behaviour) is correct. What needs building is the experience around it: a real progress UI rather than a frozen menu bar, resumable download, SHA verification, graceful handling of a tester on hotel wifi, a clear 'this is a one-time 1.5 GB download' message before it starts, and a way for Jay to hand a tester a pre-seeded cache directory. Quantized variants exist (mlx-community whisper-large-v3-turbo in 4-bit and 8-bit) and would cut the download substantially — but Gujarati and code-switched mixed-language input is precisely where quantization damage shows up first, so that should be a measured decision against his WER harness, not an assumption.
findings.evidence: Local: `du -sh ~/.cache/huggingface/hub/models--mlx-community--whisper-large-v3-turbo` → 1.5G; `du -sh .venv_old_w4k/.../mlx` → 178M. https://huggingface.co/mlx-community/whisper-large-v3-turbo/tree/main (weights.safetensors 1.61 GB). https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/813586 (notarization taking 3.5-4.5 hours for large binaries). https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/124958 (75 notarizations/day). Local: packaging/setup_app.py docstring confirms weights are deliberately not bundled.

findings.topic: Insights analytics: how to compute WPM, streaks and per-app usage with nothing leaving the Mac
findings.detail: Store a single SQLite database at ~/Library/Application Support/health.baps.w1/insights.db — explicitly NOT under ~/Documents or ~/Desktop, both of which are iCloud-synced on Jay's own setup and would silently push usage data off-device, breaking the promise by accident. Schema: a `sessions` table (id, started_at_utc, tz_offset, audio_duration_ms, wall_duration_ms, word_count, char_count, backend, model_id, language, target_bundle_id, corrections_applied) and optional pre-aggregated `daily_stats` rollups for fast dashboard loads. The single most important design rule: store counts, never text. No transcripts, no snippets, no per-word data. That is what makes 'we cannot see your dictation' structurally true rather than a policy claim. WPM: distinguish raw speaking WPM (word_count / audio_duration_ms) from effective WPM (words that survived into the target app / total wall time including correction) — the second is the number that actually sells the product and it needs the post-correction count. Streaks: derive at query time from DISTINCT local-date values computed from started_at_utc + tz_offset; never store a running streak counter, because it corrupts on clock changes, travel and DST. Per-app usage: Jay already has focus detection, so record NSWorkspace.frontmostApplication.bundleIdentifier at paste time, plus the localized display name for the UI. Retention: give the user a visible row count, a per-app delete, and a 'delete all Insights data' button that actually VACUUMs. Crash reporting: for a Developer ID app Jay gets nothing automatically — App Store Connect crash reports only exist for App Store/TestFlight apps. Crash logs land in the tester's ~/Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports/. The privacy-consistent approach is a local crash handler (faulthandler plus NSSetUncaughtExceptionHandler) writing to the app's own log directory, a menu item that reveals the file in Finder, and an explicit 'Send diagnostics' action that shows the full payload for review before anything transmits — opt-in, off by default. Bolting on Sentry or Crashpad with default settings would quietly ship stack traces, file paths containing the user's name, and environment data off-device.
findings.evidence: Design synthesis grounded in verified local facts (Jay's ~/Documents and ~/Desktop are iCloud-synced per /Users/jaypatel/Vault/CLAUDE.md and build.sh's xattr workaround) plus Apple's TCC/crash-report model. Crash-report availability limited to App Store/TestFlight: https://developer.apple.com/testflight/. Not independently verified against a citable spec — the schema and metric definitions are my recommendation, not documentation.

findings.topic: The privacy promise is the biggest unaddressed risk, and the meeting bot breaks it structurally
findings.detail: '100% on-device, nothing leaves the Mac' is already not literally true: first run fetches 1.5 GB from huggingface.co. That is benign and easily worded, but it establishes that the claim needs qualifying rather than repeating. Three planned features are harder. (1) Meeting bot joining Teams/Google Meet/Zoom: the industry-standard implementation is a server-side headless browser client that joins as a participant and streams audio to a backend — that is the opposite of on-device, and it means other people's meeting audio, captured under a product marketed as private, transits Jay's infrastructure. A local-only variant (a hidden browser instance on the user's own Mac) keeps audio on-device but is fragile, and automated participants sit awkwardly against several platforms' terms and against two-party consent recording law in some jurisdictions. This needs a product decision before it needs an engineering decision. (2) LLM text modes: Polish/Formal/Street on a small local model can stay on-device; Prompt Engineer realistically wants a frontier model, which means the user's text leaves. (3) Meeting capture itself via mic + system audio is fine on-device. Recommended wording approach: retire the single global claim and publish per-feature data-flow statements — 'Dictation is processed entirely on your Mac; audio and transcripts never leave your device.' / 'First run downloads the speech model (~1.5 GB) from Hugging Face. No audio, text or personal data is sent.' / 'Insights are computed and stored only on your Mac. We have no way to see them.' / 'Prompt Engineer sends the selected text to <provider>. It is off by default and the menu bar icon changes whenever text leaves your Mac.' Back this with a global 'Strict local' toggle that hard-fails any outbound call rather than degrading silently, and a visible network indicator. Two reasons this matters more than usual: Jay is a clinician and early testers will likely be clinicians who dictate patient material, so an unannounced network path is an information-governance incident, not a marketing quibble; and a blanket '100% on-device' claim while a shipped feature calls out is straightforwardly misleading advertising.
findings.evidence: Local: setup_app.py NSMicrophoneUsageDescription currently asserts 'Audio never leaves your computer'; docs/PACKAGING.md and setup_app.py confirm weights download from Hugging Face on first run, contradicting the absolute claim. recommendation:
Do these in order; steps 1-3 are a hard sequence because TCC grants are keyed to the signing identity and re-signing later forces every tester to manually repair permissions.

**1. Get the certificate before writing any more code.** Confirm the Apple Developer Program status of team WALY2J97BF, enrol as an individual if needed ($99, no D-U-N-S), generate the Developer ID Application certificate as Account Holder, and immediately export the private key as a .p12 to offline storage. Create the App Store Connect API key and run `xcrun notarytool store-credentials "w1-notary" --key ... --key-id ... --issuer ... --validate`. Nothing downstream works until this exists, and every day spent building on the Apple Development identity is a day of TCC state that will have to be thrown away.

**2. Fix the three signing defects, then get one notarized DMG onto a second Mac.** Add `--timestamp`. Replace `--deep` with an inside-out loop over all 336 nested Mach-O files (no entitlements on nested items), signing the outer .app last with entitlements and `--identifier health.baps.w1`. Strip `allow-jit` from the entitlements and keep `allow-unsigned-executable-memory` — sounddevice's libffi closures require it and allow-jit does not cover them. Then run the full sequence: ditto-zip, `notarytool submit --wait`, `stapler staple` the app, build the DMG from the stapled app, notarize and staple the DMG too. Validate offline with the network disconnected via `spctl -a -vvv`. Do not skip the second-Mac test — a bundle that launches on the build machine and fails everywhere else is the single most common py2app distribution failure, usually a lazily-imported module py2app's modulegraph missed.

**3. Add Sparkle before the first tester, not after.** Generate the EdDSA keypair, put SUPublicEDKey and SUFeedURL in Info.plist, drive SPUStandardUpdaterController from PyObjC, and remember Sparkle's XPC services and Autoupdate.app join the inside-out signing loop. Retrofitting an updater once testers are scattered across old builds is a support burden that compounds. Ship the notarized DMG behind a link; add a private Homebrew tap later as a convenience for technical testers, and drop official homebrew-cask from the plan entirely (75 stars / 30 forks / 30 watchers minimum, or 225 / 90 / 90 self-submitted). TestFlight is not an option at all — it requires a sandboxed Mac App Store build, and the sandbox is incompatible with Accessibility paste injection and Input Monitoring.

**4. Keep the weights out of the bundle and invest in first-run instead.** 1.5 GB verified. Bundling means 2 GB+ notarization uploads, reported multi-hour turnarounds on large binaries against a 75-per-day cap, and Sparkle re-pushing unchanged weights to every tester on every release. Build a proper download experience — visible progress, resumable, checksum-verified, a clear one-time-1.5 GB warning, and a way to hand a tester a pre-seeded cache. Evaluate the 4-bit and 8-bit MLX variants against the existing WER harness before assuming they are viable; Gujarati and code-switched input is where quantization degrades first.

**5. For meeting capture, prefer Core Audio process taps over ScreenCaptureKit.** Taps (macOS 14.4+) need only `NSAudioCaptureUsageDescription` and their own narrow TCC category, versus ScreenCaptureKit demanding the full Screen Recording grant plus a restart for what is audio-only capture. Asking a clinician for screen recording permission to transcribe a meeting is a conversation Jay does not want to have.

**6. Resolve the privacy promise now, as a product decision.** This is the finding I would escalate hardest. The current absolute claim is already inaccurate because of the model download, and the meeting bot as normally implemented — a server-side headless participant — inverts the entire proposition. Replace one global claim with per-feature data-flow statements, add a "Strict local" toggle that hard-fails outbound calls rather than degrading quietly, and add a visible indicator whenever anything leaves the machine. Build Insights on a local SQLite store under ~/Library/Application Support/health.baps.w1/ — never ~/Documents or ~/Desktop, both iCloud-synced on Jay's setup — storing counts only, never transcript text. That structural choice is what makes "we cannot see your dictation" true rather than promised. Note that Developer ID apps get no automatic crash reporting, so pair a local crash handler with an explicit opt-in "Send diagnostics" flow that shows the payload before transmitting.

Two things I could not verify and Jay should confirm himself: the Apple Developer Program membership tier for WALY2J97BF (no shell command exposes it), and the ToS and two-party-consent implications of an automated bot joining Teams/Meet/Zoom, which I did not research and which should gate that feature's scope.
